title: Multi-Bandwidth Distribution Matching Distillation: On the Equivalence of Distribution Matching Distillation and Drifting Models

paper.title: Multi-Bandwidth Distribution Matching Distillation: On the Equivalence of Distribution Matching Distillation and Drifting Models
paper.abstract:
Abstract Researchers are exploring effective one-step generative model continuously, and, Drifting Models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) , demonstrate great potential in one-step generation recently.
There are works that reveal the connection between Diffusion & Flow Style Generative Models (DFSGMs) ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ; Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) and Drifting Models ( Li and Zhu, 2026 ; Lai et al., 2026 ; Turan et al., 2026 ) . But no one has yet established a precise correspondence between the Drifting Model and the widely used distillation method- Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD/DMD2) ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ) to the best of our knowledge, even though their optimization objective formulas are virtually identical.
In this paper, we prove that by converting the velocity-field / noise-field from the pre-trained DFSGMs into the attraction force field in Drifting Models and estimating the repulsion force field from the generative distribution, training the Drifting Modelis naturally equivalent the Distribution Matching Distillation.
With this equivalent concept,
we propose an improved method based on DMD from the Drifting Model’s perspective- Multi-Bandwidth Distribution Matching Distillation (MBDMD).

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Image generation can be viewed as a distribution mapping problem: given a simple source distribution p 0 p_{0} , typically Gaussian noise, and a target data distribution p data p_{\mathrm{data}} , it seek a mapping h h such that h # ​ p 0 ≈ p data . h_{\#}p_{0}\approx p_{\mathrm{data}}. Much of the progress in generative modeling over the past decade can be understood as different ways of approaching this mapping. The most direct solution is to learn h h itself. GANs ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ) follow this idea by training a generator to map noise directly to data, with a discriminator providing the signal that distinguishes the generated distribution from the real one. This makes inference a single forward pass, but learning the mapping is difficult: the discriminator changes together with the generator, making optimization require carefully tuned parameters and additional approaches to maintain stability. Diffusion and Flow-Matching Style Generative Models (DFSGMs) ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ; Lipman et al., 2022 ) largely avoid this difficulty by changing the problem. Rather than learning the full mapping from p 0 p_{0} to p data p_{\mathrm{data}} at once, they break it into a sequence of denoising transformations along a continuous distribution path. In Flow Matching, a time-dependent velocity field specifies how samples should move at each time-step along this path, and the final mapping is obtained by integrating these local updates. This progressive formulation has proved much easier to scale to complex data distributions, but the benefit comes with a structural cost: the learned mapping is no longer executed directly and instead requires iterative inference. Recent few-step distillation methods improve inference efficiency while ensuring the quality of the generated results to a certain extent. Methods such as Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD/DMD2) ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ) start from a pretrained Diffusion Model, and train a new student generator to reach the target distribution in only a few steps or even a single step. The resulting generator therefore shifts the process from learning local variables to construct trajectories to learning more direct generation by optimizing the distance between distributions. More recently, Drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) have introduced a more explicitly designed particles perspective formulation. Instead of adversarial learning or diffusion-based transport and distillation, Drifting Model learns the distribution mapping through explicit attraction toward the target distribution and repulsion from the generated distribution adopt the concept of mean-shift ( Cheng, 1995 ) . Despite this different starting point, it again produces a generator capable of one-step generation. Moreover, the Drifting Model has demonstrated immense potential—and not merely in terms of efficiency gains. The high quality of its results has also encouraged further research efforts to build upon it ( Han et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . The formulation of the Drifting Model is based on an explicitly human-designed scheme, which raises an interesting question: what is the connection between it and other generative models? Is it merely a variant of some existing method? There already exist some works that reveal the connection between DFSGMs and Drifting Model from Score-based Generative Model view ( Lai et al., 2026 ; Turan et al., 2026 ) or second-order velocity approximation ( Li and Zhu, 2026 ) . In this work, we take a step toward this broader topic. We particularly focus on revealing the connections between DMD and Drifting models, we prove that DMD and Drifting models are theoretically identical computations under distillation of DFSGMs. Unlike other works that rely on derivations with asymptotic approximations ( Lai et al., 2026 ; Turan et al., 2026 ; Li and Zhu, 2026 ) , we provide a precise correspondence between DMD and Drifting Models with finite-sample analysis. Based on our derivations, we reformulate the computation in DMD training as that of Drifting Models, and further incorporate the Multi-Bandwidth concept from Drifting Models to improve the training paradigm of DMD. This application of the proposed theorem is named Multi-Bandwidth Distribution Matching Distillation (MBDMD). It enables faster convergence efficiency while achieving better generation quality in DMD training. In addition, the proposed derivation provides natural theoretical explanations for several existing DMD variants from the perspective of Drifting Models. To summary, our contributions are: (1) We derived the exact correspondence between DMD and Drifting Models training under finite-sample analysis. (2) The proposed derivation provides theoretical bridge from new perspectives for some DMD-related works. (3) Based on our theorem, we proposed an approach that employs multiple bandwidths to improve the training efficiency and results quality of DMD.

sections.heading: 3 Equivalence of Distribution Matching Distillation and Drifting Models
sections.text: There are works have attempted to unify the perspectives of DFSGMs and Drifting Models. The Long-Short Flow-Map (LSFM) has proved that Flow Matching is essentially the same with Drifting Models using the second-order approximation near the end point of the trajectory ( Li and Zhu, 2026 ) . Furthermore, researchers has also proved that Drifting Model optimization admits a score-based formulation ( Lai et al., 2026 ; Turan et al., 2026 ) . However, all these methods have only completed non-finite-sample analysis which requires mathematical infinite value approximation. Our derivation, on the contrary, provides an accurate transformation under finite-sample analysis. In this section, we start by introducing our formulation from the perspective of distilling a pre-trained Flow Matching Model to a one-step Drifting Model. Then, we align our derived formulation with DMD precisely. Finally, we extend this formulation to a more general view and incorporate different kinds of Diffusion Models into our paradigm.

sections.heading: 3.2 Connection with DMD
sections.text:

sections.heading: 3.4 Insight and Connection with DMD-related Studies
sections.text: Our formulation naturally provides us with many insights on how to improve DMD-related works if we use the perspective of the Drifting Model. One potential lies in how the t t is chosen in DMD. From the perspective of DMD, t t is used for adding noise and obtaining the marginal score at time t t for KL divergence optimization. However, when move the view from DMD to training Drifting Models, this t t becomes the bandwidth of the kernel function in many noise schedulers. From this perspective, the impact of varying t t on the results during DMD distillation can be reinterpreted from a noise-related Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) standpoint to a bandwidth-oriented one. For instance, works such as Flash-DMD ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , DP-DMD ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , and 1.x Distill ( Li et al., 2026 ) identified that t t significantly influences the SNR in different noise level (high-noise level for global structure and low-noise for local detail). Consequently, they employ different strategies at various noise levels to obtain better optimization signals. This allows the exact same result to be derived from a bandwidth perspective. With a large bandwidth, the attraction tends to point to the center of a large number of samples, and what is learned is general, coarse information from a large number of samples. As the bandwidth gradually decreases, fewer and more precise samples are perceived, and what is learned is detail approaching the ground truth. In addition, works like ADM ( Lu et al., 2025 ) and Phased-DMD ( Fan et al., 2025 ) improve distillation quality by adjusting the scheduling of t t and optimizing the results corresponding to different values of t t . One uses a Cubic Generator Timestep Schedule to allow more of the t t fall into the noisy phase which is the same to utilize more larger bandwidth to perceive more data. The other utilize a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to learn results under several different t t conditions, which is equivalent to having different Experts handle different perceptual bandwidths. The above works are basically aimed at solving the learning problem under the selection of t t in DMD. Through our formulation, after switching the perspective to Drifting Model, these findings can actually be explained from the perspective of the bandwidth in kernel function computation. Besides the work mentioned above, another major issue affecting DMD’s performance is that the Fake Score Model needs to be updated in real time to track the generative distribution of the student model. This makes training the Fake Score Model difficult and often affects the final quality of the distillation ( Ge et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . Our formulation proves that the score estimated by the Fake Score Model is actually the same as the repulsion force field that calculated by a special kernel function. Using the repulsion force field naturally avoids the alignment problem between the generative distributions of the Fake Score Model and the student model. However, the biggest problem is that we cannot directly calculate the kernel function in high-dimensional space because of the infamous curse of dimensionality. There exists a “free, unbiased, and lag-free” estimator for the fake score, but its available bandwidth is too narrow, roughly on the below 0.01 for t t according to Effective Sample Size (ESS) calculations. Even so, we demonstrate the feasibility of using the repulsion force field to replace fake scores with low-dimensional data. We use the common 2D checkerboard scenario to implement this, and the results are illustrated in Supplementary Materials B . We show that without the curse of dimensionality, it is achievable to address the issue of update lag in the Fake Score Model by using a repulsion force field calculated based on a special kernel function.

sections.heading: 4 Multi-Bandwidth Distribution Matching Distillation
sections.text: To bring advantageous designs from vanilla Drifting Model to DMD by our unified formulation, we analyze the unified version of kernel function (in equation 30 ) that from the conditional expectation. We hereinafter refer this kernel function as the Uni kernel. For the Uni-kernel approach, the variable σ t \sigma_{t} are theoretically functions of t t and represents the bandwidth of force calculation. Typically, σ t \sigma_{t} decreases as t t increasing. When σ t \sigma_{t} is large, the receptive field calculated by the kernel function is also very large; in this case, it is easy to learn the global structure. As σ t \sigma_{t} approaches 0 0 , the bandwidth approaches 0 0 too. At this point, the target degenerates into discrete delta spikes on the manifold, causing the model to learn the specific details of the samples. To balance these two extremes, the vanilla Drifting Model employs three different bandwidths to obtain results across varying receptive fields. This motivates our Multi-Bandwidth Distribution Matching Distillation (MBDMD). The entire MBDMD method can be simply described in one sentence: we divide the entire range of bandwidth values ( t t values in DMD) into several regions (notated as K K ) and randomly sample a t t value as bandwidth from each region which results in various bandwidths at each step of the student model training thereby effectively covering the majority of the bandwidth range.

sections.heading: 5 Experiments and Results
sections.text: We show that MBDMD not only improves the quality of the results, but also increase the training efficiency. The base setting of MBDMD uses 3 3 ( K = 3 K=3 ) different bandwidths, with the bandwidth values switching depending on different pre-trained teacher. We noticed that choosing a good range of bandwidth values is essential to improve the results quality further. However, the attempt to find a universal method for optimal bandwidth value range by only using a teacher model failed. Therefore, we ultimately chose to use the simplest method to determine the bandwidth sampling distribution, which is to align it with the sampler used during inference for the teacher model. We follow the vanilla DMD training settings on Diffusion Models with ImageNet dataset at 64 by 64 resolution. Our main experiments were conducted with pure DMD without GAN loss in order to isolate the influence of GAN loss first. Experiments (table 2 ) show that we achieved better FID results than vanilla DMD’s 410k steps with 328k optimization steps. Even considering that we need 3 forward passes per pass (the GPU power consumption of each step is equivalent to 1.15 steps of vanilla DMD), the improvement in training efficiency is substantial. When our experiment reached the same 410k steps, we obtained an FID value of 2.4697. sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we established an exact finite-sample correspondence between DMD and Drifting Models under the distillation frameworks of DFSGMs. This correspondence shows that DMD’s distribution-matching computation admits an equivalent attraction–repulsion formulation, revealing a shared theoretical basis beneath their different formulations. Beyond clarifying this connection, the derivation enables the transfer of multi-bandwidth training to DMD, yielding MBDMD and improvements in convergence and generation quality on two image generation datasets. The same theoretical framework also provides an alternative interpretation of several existing DMD variants.

sections.heading: Appendix B Using Kernel calculation to replace Fake Score Model
sections.text: In section 3.4 , we mentioned that our formulation of the equivalence of Drifting Model and DMD introduce a potential method to resolve the learning lag of online updating for the Fake Score Model in DMD. However, it is not practical in high dimension due to the curse of dimensionality. In order to prove the feasibility, we did an classical 2D toy experiment. We used the common 2D checkerboard pattern as the ground truth. First, we trained a Flow Matching Model to serve as the teacher model. Next, we conducted three different experiments, all aimed at obtaining a student model capable of one-step generation. In the first experiment, we directly used the kernel function deducted from with Flow Matching (equation 7 ) to calculate both the attrition and repulsion forces; the teacher model was not utilized in this case. In the second experiment, we replaced the attraction force with a formulation incorporating the Flow Matching velocity (equation 15 )—equivalent to the real score in DMD—while still using the Flow Matching kernel (equation 7 ) to calculate the repulsion force. This resolved the issue of update lag in the Fake Score Model. The third experiment was DMD, in which we replaced both the attraction and repulsion forces with formulations incorporating the Flow Matching velocity- specifically, the real score and fake score. The visualization of results are shown in Figure B . We can see that all three of these approaches generally yield excellent results. Figure 1 : A 2D toy experiments to show that Fake Score Model can be replaced by the repulsion kernel function calculation. In this figure, (a) is the ground-truth; (b) is the results generated by pure kernel calculation for both attraction and repulsion; (c) shows the result by transferring velocity from pretrained Flow Matching Model to calculate attraction force and use kernel calculation for repulsion; (d) is the result from DMD which using velocity from pretrained Flow Matching Model to calculate attraction force and using a online updating Fake Score Model to calculate repulsion force.

There are works that reveal the connection between Diffusion & Flow Style Generative Models (DFSGMs) ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ; Lipman et al., 2022 ; Liu et al., 2022 ) and Drifting Models ( Li and Zhu, 2026 ; Lai et al., 2026 ; Turan et al., 2026 ) . But no one has yet established a precise correspondence between the Drifting Model and the widely used distillation method- Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD/DMD2) ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ) to the best of our knowledge, even though their optimization objective formulas are virtually identical. In this paper, we prove that by converting the velocity-field / noise-field from the pre-trained DFSGMs into the attraction force field in Drifting Models and estimating the repulsion force field from the generative distribution, training the Drifting Modelis naturally equivalent the Distribution Matching Distillation. With this equivalent concept, we propose an improved method based on DMD from the Drifting Model’s perspective- Multi-Bandwidth Distribution Matching Distillation (MBDMD). Keywords: Deep Learning 1 Introduction Image generation can be viewed as a distribution mapping problem: given a simple source distribution p 0 p_{0} , typically Gaussian noise, and a target data distribution p data p_{\mathrm{data}} , it seek a mapping h h such that h # ​ p 0 ≈ p data . h_{\#}p_{0}\approx p_{\mathrm{data}}. Much of the progress in generative modeling over the past decade can be understood as different ways of approaching this mapping. The most direct solution is to learn h h itself. GANs ( Goodfellow et al., 2020 ) follow this idea by training a generator to map noise directly to data, with a discriminator providing the signal that distinguishes the generated distribution from the real one. This makes inference a single forward pass, but learning the mapping is difficult: the discriminator changes together with the generator, making optimization require carefully tuned parameters and additional approaches to maintain stability. Diffusion and Flow-Matching Style Generative Models (DFSGMs) ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020a ; Song et al., 2020b ; Lipman et al., 2022 ) largely avoid this difficulty by changing the problem. Rather than learning the full mapping from p 0 p_{0} to p data p_{\mathrm{data}} at once, they break it into a sequence of denoising transformations along a continuous distribution path. In Flow Matching, a time-dependent velocity field specifies how samples should move at each time-step along this path, and the final mapping is obtained by integrating these local updates. This progressive formulation has proved much easier to scale to complex data distributions, but the benefit comes with a structural cost: the learned mapping is no longer executed directly and instead requires iterative inference. Recent few-step distillation methods improve inference efficiency while ensuring the quality of the generated results to a certain extent. Methods such as Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD/DMD2) ( Yin et al., 2024b ; Yin et al., 2024a ) start from a pretrained Diffusion Model, and train a new student generator to reach the target distribution in only a few steps or even a single step. The resulting generator therefore shifts the process from learning local variables to construct trajectories to learning more direct generation by optimizing the distance between distributions. More recently, Drifting models ( Deng et al., 2026 ) have introduced a more explicitly designed particles perspective formulation. Instead of adversarial learning or diffusion-based transport and distillation, Drifting Model learns the distribution mapping through explicit attraction toward the target distribution and repulsion from the generated distribution adopt the concept of mean-shift ( Cheng, 1995 ) . Despite this different starting point, it again produces a generator capable of one-step generation. Moreover, the Drifting Model has demonstrated immense potential—and not merely in terms of efficiency gains. The high quality of its results has also encouraged further research efforts to build upon it ( Han et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . The formulation of the Drifting Model is based on an explicitly human-designed scheme, which raises an interesting question: what is the connection between it and other generative models? Is it merely a variant of some existing method? There already exist some works that reveal the connection between DFSGMs and Drifting Model from Score-based Generative Model view ( Lai et al., 2026 ; Turan et al., 2026 ) or second-order velocity approximation ( Li and Zhu, 2026 ) . In this work, we take a step toward this broader topic. We particularly focus on revealing the connections between DMD and Drifting models, we prove that DMD and Drifting models are theoretically identical computations under distillation of DFSGMs. Unlike other works that rely on derivations with asymptotic approximations ( Lai et al., 2026 ; Turan et al., 2026 ; Li and Zhu, 2026 ) , we provide a precise correspondence between DMD and Drifting Models with finite-sample analysis. Based on our derivations, we reformulate the computation in DMD training as that of Drifting Models, and further incorporate the Multi-Bandwidth concept from Drifting Models to improve the training paradigm of DMD. This application of the proposed theorem is named Multi-Bandwidth Distribution Matching Distillation (MBDMD). It enables faster convergence efficiency while achieving better generation quality in DMD training. In addition, the proposed derivation provides natural theoretical explanations for several existing DMD variants from the perspective of Drifting Models. To summary, our contributions are: (1) We derived the exact correspondence between DMD and Drifting Models training under finite-sample analysis. (2) The proposed derivation provides theoretical bridge from new perspectives for some DMD-related works. (3) Based on our theorem, we proposed an approach that employs multiple bandwidths to improve the training efficiency and results quality of DMD. 2 Preliminary Diffusion Models construct the transformation from real data distribution to a known noise distribution by progressively perturbing training images until their distribution approaches the tractable noise prior. During the training, it learns the reverse evolution from noise to real data across noise levels ( Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 ; Ho et al., 2020 ) . In addition to Flow Matching, Diffusion Model VP and Diffusion Model VE, all models that establish trajectories through interpolation in Gaussian distribution and real data distribution can be incorporated into our paradigm. 3.4 Insight and Connection with DMD-related Studies Our formulation naturally provides us with many insights on how to improve DMD-related works if we use the perspective of the Drifting Model. One potential lies in how the t t is chosen in DMD. From the perspective of DMD, t t is used for adding noise and obtaining the marginal score at time t t for KL divergence optimization. However, when move the view from DMD to training Drifting Models, this t t becomes the bandwidth of the kernel function in many noise schedulers. From this perspective, the impact of varying t t on the results during DMD distillation can be reinterpreted from a noise-related Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) standpoint to a bandwidth-oriented one. For instance, works such as Flash-DMD ( Chen et al., 2025 ) , DP-DMD ( Wu et al., 2026 ) , and 1.x Distill ( Li et al., 2026 ) identified that t t significantly influences the SNR in different noise level (high-noise level for global structure and low-noise for local detail). Consequently, they employ different strategies at various noise levels to obtain better optimization signals. This allows the exact same result to be derived from a bandwidth perspective. With a large bandwidth, the attraction tends to point to the center of a large number of samples, and what is learned is general, coarse information from a large number of samples. As the bandwidth gradually decreases, fewer and more precise samples are perceived, and what is learned is detail approaching the ground truth. In addition, works like ADM ( Lu et al., 2025 ) and Phased-DMD ( Fan et al., 2025 ) improve distillation quality by adjusting the scheduling of t t and optimizing the results corresponding to different values of t t . One uses a Cubic Generator Timestep Schedule to allow more of the t t fall into the noisy phase which is the same to utilize more larger bandwidth to perceive more data. The other utilize a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture to learn results under several different t t conditions, which is equivalent to having different Experts handle different perceptual bandwidths. The above works are basically aimed at solving the learning problem under the selection of t t in DMD. Through our formulation, after switching the perspective to Drifting Model, these findings can actually be explained from the perspective of the bandwidth in kernel function computation. Besides the work mentioned above, another major issue affecting DMD’s performance is that the Fake Score Model needs to be updated in real time to track the generative distribution of the student model. This makes training the Fake Score Model difficult and often affects the final quality of the distillation ( Ge et al., 2025 ; Huang et al., 2026 ) . Our formulation proves that the score estimated by the Fake Score Model is actually the same as the repulsion force field that calculated by a special kernel function.
